title: Fine-Tuning Fundamentals
description: What fine-tuning is, when to reach for it instead of RAG or prompting, the stages it comes in, and what good training data looks like.

lessons.title: What Fine-Tuning Actually Is
lessons.description: Take a pretrained model and keep training it on your own examples, so its behavior shifts toward what you need.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain what fine-tuning changes inside a model, and describe the difference between pretraining and fine-tuning in plain terms.

sections.title: 🧠 The idea
sections.content:
A pretrained LLM already knows grammar, facts, and reasoning patterns from a huge, general training run. **Fine-tuning** takes that same model and keeps training it — usually for much less time, on a much smaller, much more specific dataset — so its outputs shift toward a particular style, format, or task. Nothing architecturally new is added by default: you're adjusting the same weights, just nudging them with new examples.

Think of pretraining as someone reading a huge chunk of the internet and forming a broad, general sense of language and the world. Fine-tuning is like handing that same person a stack of your company's support tickets and saying 'now write replies like these.' They don't forget everything else they know — they just get much better and much more consistent at this one thing.

```python
# Conceptually, fine-tuning is just... more training
model = load_pretrained("base-model-7b")
for batch in your_small_specific_dataset:
    loss = model.compute_loss(batch)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()  # the same weights, nudged toward your examples
```

sections.title: 🔧 Why it matters
sections.content: Base pretrained models are surprisingly bad at doing what you actually want by default. Ask a raw pretrained (non-instruction-tuned) model a question and it might continue your question with more questions, because 'continue the text' is literally all it learned to do. Fine-tuning is the tool that turns a general next-token predictor into something that reliably follows instructions, adopts a tone, sticks to a format, or handles a narrow domain — which is why almost every model you've used as a product (ChatGPT, Claude, etc.) started as a pretrained base and was then fine-tuned (often several times, in several stages) before it ever reached you.

sections.title: 📌 The three big use cases
sections.content:
Fine-tuning tends to solve one of three problems:

- **Format and style** — get outputs to consistently follow a schema, a tone, a house style, or a specific output structure.
- **Behavior and instruction-following** — teach the model to be an assistant that follows instructions, uses tools, or refuses certain requests, rather than just continuing text.
- **Narrow domain adaptation** — make the model fluent in a specialized vocabulary or task pattern (legal contract clauses, radiology reports, a company's internal jargon) that's underrepresented in general pretraining data.

Notice what's missing from that list: 'teaching the model new facts it doesn't already know.' That's a common misconception, and it's the subject of the next lesson.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming fine-tuning adds new architecture or abilities the base model never had.** It only continues training existing weights — it can't give a model a capability, like vision or tool use, it had no mechanism for in the first place.

**Treating fine-tuning as a way to teach a model new facts.** It nudges behavior, not a knowledge base — the next lesson covers why RAG is usually the better tool for facts.

**Forgetting that a base model already has most of the capability you need.** Fine-tuning's job is to demonstrate exactly the behavior you want, not to teach language or reasoning from scratch — over-training on a task the model can basically already do wastes data and risks overfitting.

questions.question: What does fine-tuning do to a pretrained model's weights?
options: It replaces them entirely with new weights
It continues training them on a smaller, more specific dataset
It freezes them and adds a lookup table instead
It compresses them to a smaller model size
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning continues training the same weights on new, usually much smaller and more specific, data — it doesn't discard or replace the model.

questions.question: Why are raw pretrained (non-instruction-tuned) models often bad at following instructions directly?
options: They have too few parameters
Their only trained objective was predicting the next token in text, not following commands
They were never exposed to English
They can't process more than one sentence
questions.explanation: Pretraining only teaches next-token prediction. Following instructions reliably is a behavior that has to be taught afterward, typically via instruction fine-tuning.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the three main use cases for fine-tuning described in this lesson?
options: Getting consistent output format or tone
Teaching instruction-following behavior
Adapting to a narrow domain vocabulary
Injecting large amounts of new factual knowledge
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning is not a great tool for injecting lots of new facts — that's better handled by retrieval (RAG). Fine-tuning shines at style, behavior, and narrow domain fluency.

questions.question: In this lesson's conceptual code example, what does the training loop do with each batch from the small, specific dataset?
options: Computes a loss, backpropagates it, and steps the optimizer to nudge the existing weights
Deletes the batch without using it
Replaces the model's architecture with a new one
Only stores the batch for later, with no training happening
questions.explanation: The lesson's code example shows a standard training loop: compute loss, call backward(), and step the optimizer — the same fundamental mechanism as pretraining, just applied to a smaller dataset.

questions.question: According to this lesson's analogy, what does pretraining correspond to, compared to fine-tuning?
options: Someone reading a huge chunk of the internet and forming a broad, general sense of language and the world
Someone being handed a stack of support tickets and told to write replies like them
Someone forgetting everything they previously knew
Someone being given a completely different set of instructions with no prior knowledge
questions.explanation: The lesson's analogy maps pretraining to broad general reading, and fine-tuning to the more specific, narrower task of learning to write in a particular style from a smaller set of examples.

questions.question: Why does the lesson say almost every product model (like ChatGPT or Claude) went through fine-tuning before reaching users?
options: Because a raw pretrained model would just continue text unreliably rather than acting like a helpful assistant
Because fine-tuning is required to increase a model's total parameter count
Because pretraining alone always produces a fully instruction-following assistant
Because fine-tuning is only used for translation tasks
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that pretrained models default to continuing text rather than following instructions, so fine-tuning (often through multiple stages) is what turns that into assistant-like behavior.

questions.question: Why does this lesson warn against assuming fine-tuning can give a model an entirely new architectural capability?
options: Because fine-tuning only continues training existing weights — it can't add a mechanism the model never had, like vision, from scratch
Because fine-tuning always redesigns the model's underlying architecture
Because new capabilities are always added automatically during fine-tuning
Because architecture and weights are unrelated to what fine-tuning changes
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is assuming fine-tuning can add fundamentally new abilities, when it can only adjust weights within the model's existing architecture.

questions.question: Why might over-training a model on a task it can basically already do waste data and risk overfitting?
options: Because fine-tuning's job is to demonstrate the target behavior clearly, and it doesn't need to reteach language or reasoning the base model already has
Because a base model never has any relevant capability before fine-tuning
Because overfitting only occurs when a dataset is too small, never when it's redundant
Because fine-tuning always requires as much data as possible regardless of the base model's existing skill
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is forgetting the base model's existing capability, since fine-tuning data should demonstrate the desired behavior rather than re-teach something the model can already mostly do.

lessons.title: Fine-Tuning vs. RAG vs. Prompting
lessons.description: Three different tools for three different problems — and picking the wrong one wastes weeks.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, given a real-world requirement, you can decide whether prompting, RAG, or fine-tuning (or some combination) is the right first move.

sections.title: 🧠 Three levers, three jobs
sections.content:
**Prompting** changes what you ask the model to do, per request — no training involved, instant to change, but limited by what the model already knows and can do. **RAG** (retrieval-augmented generation) changes what the model can see, by pulling relevant documents into the context window at request time — great for facts and knowledge that go stale or that you don't want baked into weights. **Fine-tuning** changes what the model does by default, by adjusting its weights — best for behavior, style, and format, not for facts.

A useful mental model: prompting is like giving someone instructions right before a task. RAG is like handing them a reference book to consult while doing it. Fine-tuning is like sending them through months of on-the-job training so the behavior becomes automatic.

```python
# The same problem, three different levers
prompt_only = "Answer in JSON: {question}"                 # per-request instruction
rag_answer  = generate(prompt, context=retrieve(question))  # inject facts at request time
ft_answer   = finetuned_model.generate(question)             # behavior is now the default
```

sections.title: ⚠️ The classic mistake: fine-tuning for facts
sections.content: A very common failure mode: a team wants the model to 'know about our product docs' and reaches straight for fine-tuning. They fine-tune on the docs, and the model does absorb some facts — but unreliably, with no way to cite sources, no way to update a single fact without retraining, and a real risk of the model confidently hallucinating plausible-sounding but wrong details it half-learned. Weeks later they discover that RAG — just retrieving the relevant doc snippet and putting it in the prompt — gives more accurate, easily-updatable, citable answers with far less effort. This is exactly why RAG existed as a course before this one: retrieval is usually the right default for 'the model needs to know X.'

sections.title: ✅ A practical decision order
sections.content: Start with prompting — can better instructions, examples in the prompt (few-shot), or a system prompt solve it? If the problem is 'the model doesn't know something,' reach for RAG next — feed it the facts at query time. Only reach for fine-tuning when the problem is about consistent behavior, format, tone, or a skill that's hard to describe in a prompt (like always emitting valid JSON matching your exact schema, or reliably using your company's specific tool-calling conventions). In real systems, these combine: a fine-tuned model that's also given retrieved context, driven by a well-designed prompt, is extremely common.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Reaching for fine-tuning before trying prompting or RAG.** Fine-tuning is the most expensive and slowest lever to pull — it should usually be the last one tried, not the first.

**Fine-tuning to inject facts instead of using RAG.** Baked-in facts are unreliable, uncitable, and expensive to update — retrieval solves all three problems better and cheaper.

**Treating the three tools as mutually exclusive.** Production systems routinely combine a fine-tuned model, retrieved context, and a well-designed prompt — the question is rarely 'which one' but 'which combination.'

questions.question: A team wants their assistant to always answer using the latest version of their internal wiki, which changes daily. What's the best first approach?
options: Fine-tune on the wiki content
Use RAG to retrieve the relevant wiki pages at query time
Prompt engineering alone with no external data
Increase the model's parameter count
questions.explanation: Fast-changing factual content is exactly what RAG is built for — retrieve the current version at query time rather than baking a stale snapshot into weights via fine-tuning.

questions.question: Which problem is fine-tuning best suited to solve?
options: The model needs access to today's stock prices
The model needs to consistently output a specific JSON schema in your house style
The model needs to look up rarely-changing company facts
The model needs more context window space
questions.explanation: Consistent format, tone, and behavior are exactly what fine-tuning is good at — it's a poor tool for facts, freshness, or context length.

questions.question: What is a key risk of fine-tuning on a document set purely to teach the model "facts" instead of using RAG?
options: The model becomes too slow to run
The model may hallucinate half-learned details with no way to cite or easily update individual facts
The model loses the ability to follow instructions entirely
It's technically impossible to fine-tune on documents
questions.explanation: Facts baked into weights via fine-tuning are unreliable, not citable, and expensive to update — RAG's retrieved snippets solve all three problems better.

questions.question: In this lesson's code example, what does the rag_answer line pass to generate() that prompt_only does not?
options: A context argument built from retrieve(question)
A completely different model checkpoint
A larger temperature value
A hardcoded JSON schema
questions.explanation: The lesson's code example shows rag_answer calling generate with context=retrieve(question), injecting retrieved facts at request time — something the prompt_only line doesn't do.

questions.question: According to this lesson's analogy, what does fine-tuning correspond to, compared to prompting and RAG?
options: Sending someone through months of on-the-job training so the behavior becomes automatic
Giving someone instructions right before a task
Handing someone a reference book to consult while working
Doing nothing at all and hoping for the best
questions.explanation: The lesson's analogy maps fine-tuning to extended on-the-job training that makes a behavior automatic, contrasted with prompting's per-request instructions and RAG's reference-book lookup.

questions.question: Why does this lesson recommend starting with prompting before considering RAG or fine-tuning?
options: Because it's the cheapest and fastest lever to try, and better instructions or few-shot examples might already solve the problem
Because prompting always produces strictly better results than RAG or fine-tuning
Because prompting is the only approach that can ever handle factual questions
Because RAG and fine-tuning can never be combined with prompting
questions.explanation: The lesson's decision order starts with prompting precisely because it's the fastest, cheapest thing to try before reaching for retrieval or the much heavier investment of fine-tuning.

questions.question: Why does this lesson call reaching for fine-tuning before trying prompting or RAG a mistake?
options: Because fine-tuning is the most expensive and slowest lever to pull, and should usually be tried last, not first
Because fine-tuning is always the cheapest and fastest option available
Because prompting and RAG can never actually solve any real problem
Because fine-tuning has no cost or time investment associated with it
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is skipping straight to fine-tuning, when its cost and slowness make it the tool to reach for last, after cheaper options have been tried.

questions.question: Why does this lesson warn against treating prompting, RAG, and fine-tuning as mutually exclusive choices?
options: Because production systems routinely combine a fine-tuned model, retrieved context, and a well-designed prompt together
Because using more than one of these techniques at once is technically impossible
Because combining these techniques always produces worse results than using just one
Because RAG and fine-tuning are actually identical techniques with no meaningful difference
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is treating this as an either-or choice, when real systems commonly combine all three rather than picking exactly one.

lessons.title: The Types of Fine-Tuning
lessons.description: Full fine-tuning, instruction tuning, and preference tuning are three different stages, not three interchangeable options.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can name the main stages of fine-tuning a modern LLM goes through and explain what each stage is responsible for.

sections.title: 🏗️ Full fine-tuning
sections.content:
**Full fine-tuning** updates every parameter in the model. It's the most flexible and can produce the biggest behavior shifts, but it's expensive — you need enough GPU memory to hold the full model plus optimizer states plus gradients, which for a large model can mean many high-end GPUs. It also risks **catastrophic forgetting**: aggressively overwriting weights can degrade capabilities the model had before, if you're not careful with learning rate and data mix. Because of the cost, full fine-tuning is used less often today than parameter-efficient methods, which the next module covers in depth.

```python
# Full fine-tuning: every parameter is trainable
for param in model.parameters():
    param.requires_grad = True
# Memory needed: model weights + gradients + optimizer states,
# roughly 3-4x the model's own size for a full fine-tune
```

sections.title: 📋 Instruction tuning (SFT)
sections.content: **Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)** on (instruction, response) pairs is the stage that turns a base pretrained model into something that follows instructions and behaves like an assistant. This is typically the first fine-tuning stage after pretraining, and it's what most people mean by 'fine-tuning' when they're building a task-specific assistant on top of an already-instruction-tuned model.

sections.title: 🎚️ Preference tuning (RLHF / DPO and friends)
sections.content: After a model can follow instructions, there's usually a further stage that shapes *which* of several plausible responses it should prefer — more helpful, more honest, less harmful, matching a particular tone. This uses preference data (pairs of responses where one is marked better) rather than single 'correct' answers, and includes methods like RLHF and DPO, covered in depth in a later module. The three stages roughly build on each other: pretraining gives general capability, SFT gives instruction-following, preference tuning gives refinement and alignment.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Treating full fine-tuning as the default choice.** Its GPU memory cost and forgetting risk make it the exception today, not the rule — parameter-efficient methods (next module) handle most real use cases.

**Confusing SFT with preference tuning.** SFT trains on single correct-answer examples; preference tuning trains on comparisons between responses — they use different data and solve different problems.

**Skipping straight to preference tuning without a solid instruction-tuned base.** Preference tuning refines which of several already-reasonable responses is better — it isn't a substitute for teaching basic instruction-following first.

questions.question: What is the main risk of full fine-tuning compared to parameter-efficient methods?
options: It cannot change model behavior at all
It's expensive in GPU memory and risks catastrophic forgetting of prior capabilities
It only works on models under 1 billion parameters
It requires no training data
questions.explanation: Full fine-tuning updates every weight, which needs substantial compute/memory and can overwrite useful prior behavior if not done carefully — hence the appeal of PEFT methods covered next module.

questions.question: What does supervised fine-tuning (SFT) typically use as training data?
options: Pairs of (instruction, response) examples
Pairs of (better response, worse response) preference comparisons
Raw unlabeled internet text
Only numerical embeddings
questions.explanation: SFT trains on instruction-response pairs to teach the model to follow instructions — this is what turns a base model into an assistant-like model.

questions.question: What distinguishes preference tuning (like RLHF or DPO) from instruction tuning (SFT)?
options: Preference tuning uses comparisons between responses (which is better) rather than single correct-answer examples
Preference tuning happens before pretraining
Preference tuning removes the need for any prior training stage
Preference tuning only works on image models
questions.explanation: Preference tuning refines behavior using relative judgments — 'response A is better than response B' — building on top of a model that has already learned to follow instructions via SFT.

questions.question: In this lesson's code example, what happens when every parameter's requires_grad is set to True?
options: The model performs full fine-tuning, making all parameters trainable
The model becomes permanently frozen with no parameters trainable
Only the embedding layer becomes trainable
The model's architecture is deleted
questions.explanation: The lesson's code example shows setting requires_grad = True on every parameter as the defining mechanic of full fine-tuning: everything is updated during training.

questions.question: According to this lesson's code comment, roughly how much memory does full fine-tuning need relative to the model's own size?
options: Roughly 3-4x the model's own size
Exactly the same as the model's own size, with nothing extra
Roughly half of the model's own size
No additional memory beyond storing the model weights
questions.explanation: The lesson's code comment explicitly estimates full fine-tuning memory at roughly 3-4x the model's size, accounting for weights, gradients, and optimizer states.

questions.question: According to this lesson, what does pretraining contribute in the overall three-stage progression?
options: General capability, which SFT and preference tuning then build on
Preference alignment, which pretraining supposedly does before any other stage
Nothing; pretraining is unrelated to the fine-tuning stages
Instruction-following behavior directly, with no further stages needed
questions.explanation: The lesson describes the three stages as building on each other: pretraining provides general capability, SFT adds instruction-following, and preference tuning adds refinement.

questions.question: Why does this lesson call treating full fine-tuning as the default choice a mistake?
options: Because its GPU memory cost and forgetting risk make it the exception today, with parameter-efficient methods handling most real use cases
Because full fine-tuning has no meaningful cost or risk compared to other methods
Because parameter-efficient methods are always strictly worse than full fine-tuning
Because full fine-tuning is required for every single fine-tuning task
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is defaulting to full fine-tuning, when its cost and forgetting risk make parameter-efficient methods the more common real-world choice.

questions.question: Why does this lesson warn against skipping straight to preference tuning without a solid instruction-tuned base?
options: Because preference tuning refines which of several already-reasonable responses is better, and isn't a substitute for teaching basic instruction-following first
Because preference tuning can only be applied to models that have never been trained at all
Because instruction tuning and preference tuning are actually the exact same process
Because preference tuning always works equally well regardless of the model's starting capability
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is skipping SFT, since preference tuning assumes a model that can already produce reasonable responses to compare and refine.

lessons.title: Fine-Tuning Data: Quality Over Quantity
lessons.description: A few hundred excellent examples reliably beat tens of thousands of sloppy ones.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can describe what makes a fine-tuning dataset good, and identify common data quality problems before they waste a training run.

sections.title: 📊 Less data than you think, if it's good
sections.content: One of the most reproduced findings in fine-tuning research is that a small, carefully curated dataset (hundreds to low thousands of examples) often outperforms a much larger but noisier one, especially for instruction tuning and style adaptation. The model already has enormous general capability from pretraining — fine-tuning data's job isn't to teach it language, it's to demonstrate exactly the behavior you want, consistently and correctly, so the signal is clean.

sections.title: 🧹 What 'good' data looks like
sections.content:
- **Consistent formatting** — the same structure and conventions across every example, since inconsistency is itself a pattern the model will learn.
- **Correctness** — every example should be an output you'd actually be happy to see the model produce; a single wrong or low-quality example teaches the model a bad habit just as effectively as a good one.
- **Diversity within scope** — enough varied phrasing and edge cases that the model generalizes the underlying skill, not just memorizes exact input-output pairs.
- **Deduplication** — near-duplicate examples inflate apparent dataset size without adding real signal, and can cause overfitting to a narrow pattern.

```python
# A minimal quality check before training
def check_dataset(examples):
    assert len(examples) == len(set(map(str, examples))), "duplicates found"
    for ex in examples:
        assert ex["output"], "empty output"
        assert ex["format"] == examples[0]["format"], "inconsistent format"
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Mixing inconsistent formats or tones across examples.** The model can't tell what 'the standard' actually is if every example looks different.

**Including auto-generated examples that were never reviewed by a human.** This silently bakes errors into the model just as effectively as a genuine mistake would.

**Having far too many easy examples and almost none of the edge cases that matter in production.** A dataset that doesn't reflect real usage teaches a skill that doesn't transfer.

**Not holding out a validation set.** Without one, there's no way to tell real improvement from overfitting during training.

questions.question: According to widely reproduced fine-tuning findings, what usually matters more for a good result?
options: Dataset size above all else
Data quality and consistency, even with a small dataset
Using the largest possible base model
Training for as many epochs as possible regardless of data
questions.explanation: A small, clean, consistent dataset routinely beats a large noisy one — fine-tuning mostly needs to demonstrate the target behavior clearly, not teach language from scratch.

questions.question: Why is deduplication important in a fine-tuning dataset?
options: It makes the JSON file smaller
Near-duplicate examples inflate apparent size without adding signal and can cause overfitting
It removes the need for a validation set
It's required by most training frameworks or the job will fail
questions.explanation: Duplicated or near-duplicate examples don't add new information; they just concentrate the model's attention on one narrow pattern, risking overfitting.

questions.question: What's a common data mistake mentioned in this lesson?
options: Reviewing every training example by hand
Holding out a validation set
Including auto-generated examples that were never reviewed for correctness
Using consistent formatting throughout
questions.explanation: Unreviewed auto-generated data can silently bake in errors that the model will faithfully learn — every one of the other options is a good practice, not a mistake.

questions.question: In this lesson's code example, what does the check_dataset function verify about the examples?
options: That there are no duplicates, no empty outputs, and consistent formatting across examples
That the dataset contains at least one million examples
That every example is written in a different format from the others
That the dataset has been translated into multiple languages
questions.explanation: The lesson's code example shows check_dataset asserting no duplicates, non-empty outputs, and consistent formatting — a minimal quality gate before training.

questions.question: According to this lesson, why doesn't fine-tuning data need to 'teach the model language' the way pretraining does?
options: Because the model already has enormous general capability from pretraining, so fine-tuning data's job is just to demonstrate the target behavior clearly
Because fine-tuning data is always written in a completely different language than pretraining data
Because fine-tuning never actually changes any of the model's behavior
Because pretraining and fine-tuning use the exact same dataset every time
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that pretraining already gave the model general language capability, so fine-tuning data only needs to demonstrate the specific target behavior clearly and consistently.

questions.question: Why does this lesson say diversity within scope matters for a fine-tuning dataset?
options: Because enough varied phrasing and edge cases helps the model generalize the underlying skill rather than just memorize exact input-output pairs
Because diversity always increases the total size of the dataset with no other effect
Because a dataset with no diversity at all always produces the best possible results
Because diversity has no relationship to whether a model generalizes or memorizes
questions.explanation: The lesson lists diversity within scope as one of the traits of good data, specifically because it helps the model learn the general skill rather than overfit to a narrow set of exact examples.

questions.question: Why does this lesson warn against having far too many easy examples and almost none of the edge cases that matter in production?
options: Because a dataset that doesn't reflect real usage teaches a skill that doesn't transfer to what the model will actually face
Because edge cases are never actually encountered in real production usage
Because easy examples always teach the model more than edge cases would
Because dataset composition has no effect on how well a fine-tuned model performs in production
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is over-representing easy cases, since a dataset skewed away from real production patterns produces a skill that doesn't generalize to actual usage.

questions.question: Why does this lesson recommend holding out a validation set during fine-tuning?
options: Because without one, there's no way to tell real improvement from overfitting during training
Because a validation set is only useful for full fine-tuning, never for parameter-efficient methods
Because holding out data always reduces the final model's quality with no benefit
Because validation sets are only relevant for preference tuning, not supervised fine-tuning
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is skipping a validation set, since it's what actually distinguishes genuine improvement from the model simply overfitting to the training examples.
